name: Local Data Projects
title: Local Data Projects
answer: Local data projects have students collect their own observations outdoors, such as plants, animals, weather, or water quality, then use AI to help identify species and organize the data. The approach matters because the data belongs to the students, making the work meaningful, and it shows that real data is often messy, incomplete, and worth checking. The main practical choice is matching the tool to the student's age.

sections.body: Local data projects turn the schoolyard or a nearby creek into a source of scientific evidence that students gather themselves. A class might record the plants and animals it sees, follow local weather, or measure water quality. AI tools can then assist with identifying species and arranging what the class has collected. The point is not to replace student observation but to help students work with their own observations and look for patterns. This matters because the data is meaningful to the students and because it teaches that real data is messy, incomplete, and worth checking.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a class begins outdoors by collecting observations, such as plants and animals in the schoolyard, local weather, or water quality from a nearby creek. AI can help identify species and organize the data, and students can then use Google Sheets to look for patterns. The text gives two age bands for tools. Younger students can use Seek, which identifies species without an account and without collecting personal data. Older students can use iNaturalist, which requires users to be 13 or older unless a parent gives permission, and a teacher can also ask AI to suggest questions the data might answer, for instance whether particular birds are seen more after rain.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not provide a research study or an evidence label for this idea. Its only figure reference is Figure 8.4, which shows the difference between iNaturalist and Seek. Beyond that, the support comes from practice rather than research, so the idea rests on classroom use and the described tools rather than on a cited study or finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits around age and privacy. iNaturalist requires users to be 13 or older unless a parent gives permission. Observations on iNaturalist are visible to others by default, so older students should set sensitive locations to obscured or private before posting. For younger students, Seek avoids an account and does not collect personal data. The choice of tool by age, the decision about location settings, and the judgment about which questions to ask remain with the teacher or student rather than the AI.
